chapters.title: The Friction
chapters.teaser_text: Before mobile-first challengers arrived, sending money across borders ran through a patchwork of banks, wire services, and storefront agents.
chapters.icon: <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M2 12h20M12 2v20"/><path d="m17 7-5-5-5 5M17 17l-5 5-5-5"/></svg>
chapters.deep_dive_html:
Before mobile-first challengers arrived, sending money across borders ran through a patchwork of banks, wire services, and storefront agents (Western Union, MoneyGram, informal hawala networks). For migrant workers, the experience was defined by five recurring pain points:

  • High, opaque fees — flat fees plus hidden markups on the exchange rate, often stacked together
  • Poor exchange rates — customers frequently didn't know the real mid-market rate they were losing money against
  • Slow settlement — transfers could take several days to reach a recipient
  • Limited receiving options — many corridors to emerging-market countries had few or no reliable payout points
  • No visibility or trust — senders had little to no way of tracking whether money had arrived, which matters enormously when a transfer is rent or medicine money

This friction was felt most acutely by immigrants and migrant workers — people living and working in a wealthier country while supporting family back home. For many recipient households, these transfers weren't discretionary; they were a lifeline for food, school fees, and medical care. Remitly's own founding narrative traces directly back to this group: co-founder Matt Oppenheimer witnessed it firsthand while working in Nairobi, Kenya, where he saw how painful, expensive, and unreliable it was for people to send money to loved ones internationally — even to the point where fees and exchange-rate practices felt close to exploitative.

chapters.title: The Founder(s)
chapters.teaser_text: Three founders, one shared vision: what if remittances didn't have to be broken?
chapters.icon: <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M17 21v-2a4 4 0 0 0-4-4H5a4 4 0 0 0-4 4v2"/><circle cx="9" cy="7" r="4"/><path d="M23 21v-2a4 4 0 0 0-3-3.87"/><path d="M16 3.13a4 4 0 0 1 0 7.75"/></svg>
chapters.deep_dive_html:
Remitly was founded in May 2011 in Seattle, Washington, by Matt Oppenheimer, Josh Hug, and Shivaas Gulati — originally under the name BeamIt Mobile, rebranded Remitly in August 2012.

The company incubated through Highway 12 Ventures (Idaho) and the Techstars Seattle accelerator before launching properly in Seattle — which is why Seattle remains Remitly's headquarters today.

chapters.title: The Business Model
chapters.teaser_text: Transaction fees and FX spread: the dual engines of a multi-billion dollar platform.
chapters.icon: <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10"/><path d="M12 16v-8"/><path d="M9.5 9.5 12 12l2.5-2.5"/></svg>
chapters.deep_dive_html:
Remitly makes money in two primary ways, plus a growing set of newer product lines:

  • Transaction fees — historically roughly 40% of revenue.
  • Foreign exchange (FX) spread — generally roughly 60% of revenue, representing the markup between the wholesale exchange rate and the retail rate offered to customers.
  • Newer ancillary revenue lines (2025–2026): Remitly One (membership), Remitly Flex (buy-now-pay-later), Remitly Wallet, and Remitly Business (B2B).

Who actually pays? Overwhelmingly, the sender — typically an individual immigrant or migrant worker living in a higher-income country — pays the transaction fee and absorbs the FX spread. The recipient generally receives the full converted amount with no separate fee.

Financial scale: full-year 2024 revenue was ~$1.26 billion (+34% YoY); full-year 2025 revenue reached ~$1.6 billion; Q1 2026 revenue was $452.8 million. Remitly posted its first GAAP-profitable quarter since its 2021 IPO in Q1 2025. Gross margin runs around 60%.

chapters.title: Geography & Scale
chapters.teaser_text: From a niche mobile-first challenger in Seattle to a global payments network spanning six continents.
chapters.icon: <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10"/><path d="M12 2a15.3 15.3 0 0 1 4 10 15.3 15.3 0 0 1-4 10 15.3 15.3 0 0 1-4-10 15.3 15.3 0 0 1 4-10z"/><path d="M2 12h20"/></svg>
chapters.deep_dive_html:
Remitly started as a small team in Seattle, Washington, in 2011. The company grew from a niche mobile-first challenger sending money from a handful of "send" countries into emerging-market "receive" countries, into a global cross-border payments network. Key scale milestones:

  • September 23, 2021: Remitly went public on the Nasdaq under ticker RELY.
  • 2025–2026: the platform serves more than 9 million active customers, reaches more than 175 countries, and supports transfers in more than 100 currencies.
  • The company employs roughly 3,200 people globally (as of mid-2026).
  • Recent geographic expansion includes obtaining a UAE central bank (CBUAE) license and extending Remitly Business from the U.S. into the U.K. and Canada.

chapters.title: Status Today
chapters.teaser_text: A publicly traded, profitable incumbent undergoing a classic leadership transition.
chapters.icon: <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M22 12h-4l-3 9L9 3l-3 9H2"/></svg>
chapters.deep_dive_html:
Status: actively operating and publicly traded on the Nasdaq under RELY, with a market capitalization in the range of $4.5–4.7 billion as of mid-2026.

The most significant recent development is a leadership transition: in February 2026, Sebastian J. Gunningham was appointed CEO, succeeding co-founder Matt Oppenheimer, who moved into the role of Chairman of the Board. This is a classic "founder-to-professional-CEO" transition, common once a founder-led startup has scaled into a large, mature public company.

Under new leadership, Remitly reported record Q1 2026 revenue of $452.8 million, beating analyst consensus, alongside continued profitability. The company is also visibly diversifying beyond its original single remittance product into B2B, membership, and credit.

founders.name: Matt Oppenheimer
founders.background: Dartmouth College (B.A.), Harvard Business School (MBA). Barclays (2009–2011) leading mobile banking in Nairobi, Kenya.
founders.personal_connection: Living in Nairobi, he personally experienced and observed how painful, slow, and expensive it was for people to move money across borders. He was told to 'fall in love with a problem you want to solve, not the solution.'

founders.name: Josh Hug
founders.background: Co-founder/CEO of Shelfari (acquired by Amazon in 2008). Joined Remitly initially as a Techstars mentor.
founders.personal_connection: Family living abroad meant he had firsthand experience with the difficulty of cross-border money movement.

founders.name: Shivaas Gulati
founders.personal_connection: Connected with Matt before Techstars to help turn the idea into a working mobile-first product.

milestones.description: First GAAP profitable quarter in Q1 2025.
